lessons.title: Write a professional property listing from rough notes with Claude
lessons.summary: Turn messy walkthrough notes into a polished, accurate listing description without inventing details that aren't in your notes.
lessons.goal: Turn a set of rough property notes into a publish-ready listing description that contains only verified facts.
lessons.whyItMatters: Listing copy is often written late at night from scribbled notes or a phone memo between showings. A tool that writes fast is only useful if it doesn't add square footage, upgrades, or school-district claims you never gave it — one invented fact in a listing can trigger a buyer complaint, a contract dispute, or a fair-housing issue. Learning to constrain the AI to your source notes turns it into a fast, safe first-draft writer instead of a liability.
lessons.beforeYouStart: Have a Claude account open (claude.ai or the app). Gather your rough notes for one property: room count, condition, upgrades, price, and anything the seller told you.
steps: Open a new chat in Claude (or a Project if you keep one per listing).
Paste your raw notes exactly as you took them — bullet points, fragments, and abbreviations are fine.
Use the guardrail prompt below, which tells Claude to use only the facts you provided.
Specify the target length, tone, and destination (MLS, Zillow, social).
Read the draft line by line against your original notes and delete or flag anything not sourced from them.
Ask Claude for a second, shorter version for social media using the same verified facts.
Save the approved copy in your listing file.
lessons.prompt:
You are helping me write a real estate listing description.

STRICT RULE: Use only the facts contained in the notes below. Do not invent, assume, or embellish any detail — no square footage, upgrades, school ratings, distances, or amenities that are not explicitly stated. If a fact that would normally appear in a listing is missing (e.g., square footage, year built), do not guess or write around it — list it under "Missing facts to confirm" instead.

My raw notes:
[PASTE NOTES]

Write:
1. A 150-200 word MLS-style listing description in a warm, professional tone (no exclamation-mark hype, no clichés like "won't last long").
2. A one-sentence headline for the listing.
3. A "Missing facts to confirm" list of anything you needed but wasn't in my notes.

Audience: buyers browsing listing sites. Do not mention price unless I include it in the notes.
lessons.explanation: The prompt works because it states the constraint twice — once as a rule, once as an instruction to surface gaps instead of filling them — which is what stops the model from smoothing over missing information with a plausible-sounding guess. Splitting the output into headline, body, and a missing-facts list also makes the draft easy to audit at a glance: you can check the missing-facts list first, since anything you didn't confirm should show up there rather than in the description itself. Asking for a specific tone and word count keeps the draft close to what you'll actually paste into MLS without heavy editing.
lessons.example:
Rough notes: "27 Aspen Grove Lane Unit 4B. 2 bed 2 bath condo. Kitchen redone 2 years ago, quartz counters, stainless appliances. Private balcony off living room, gets afternoon sun. In-unit washer dryer. One assigned parking spot, #14. HOA $310/mo covers water, trash, exterior. Building has elevator. Seller motivated, relocating for work."

Expected output: a 150-200 word description that mentions the redone kitchen, quartz counters, stainless appliances, private balcony, in-unit laundry, assigned parking, and the elevator building — and puts square footage, year built, and asking price under "Missing facts to confirm" since none were in the notes. It should not mention the seller's relocation (personal/negotiating information, not a listing fact) or invent a walk score or nearby amenities.
lessons.exercise: In your own Claude account, paste real (or practice) rough notes from one of your current or recent listings using the prompt above, and generate the description, headline, and missing-facts list.
lessons.expectedResult: A ready-to-edit listing description and headline, plus an accurate list of any facts you still need to confirm before publishing — with nothing in the description that isn't traceable to your notes.
commonMistakes: Pasting notes that are already polished, which hides whether the guardrail is actually working — test it once with genuinely rough notes.
Skipping the "Missing facts to confirm" list instead of using it as a pre-publish checklist.
Forgetting to specify the destination platform, so the tone and length don't match where you'll actually paste it.
Publishing the first draft without reading it against the original notes line by line.
lessons.proTip: Save this prompt as custom instructions in a Claude Project named after your listing pipeline — you'll skip retyping the guardrail every time and can drop new notes straight into the project.

lessons.title: Improve an existing property description with Claude
lessons.summary: Take a bland or dated listing description and rewrite it to be sharper and more compelling while keeping every fact accurate.
lessons.goal: Rewrite an existing property description so it reads better without changing or adding any facts.
lessons.whyItMatters: Listings often get re-marketed after weeks with no activity, or an agent inherits a co-listing with dull copy. Rewriting for tone and flow is a fast win, but it's easy for an AI rewrite to quietly change a fact — turning "updated kitchen" into "fully renovated kitchen," for instance. Learning to separate "improve the writing" from "add new facts" keeps rewrites both better and defensible.
steps: Paste the current listing description exactly as it is.
Tell Claude what's underperforming — too generic, too long, buried lead, weak headline.
Use the rewrite prompt, which locks Claude to the existing facts and asks for a fact-diff.
Compare the "Facts changed or added" list against the original and reject anything on it that isn't true.
Ask for 2-3 headline options and pick the one that fits your MLS character limit.
Proofread the final copy for tone consistency with your brokerage's voice.
lessons.prompt:
Here is my current listing description:
[PASTE CURRENT DESCRIPTION]

Rewrite it to be more engaging and specific while following these rules:
- Do not add any fact, feature, upgrade, or claim that is not already stated in the text above.
- You may reorder, cut filler, tighten sentences, and replace generic phrases (e.g., "great location") with more vivid ones that describe the SAME fact more specifically.
- Keep length to roughly [TARGET WORD COUNT] words.
- Tone: [e.g., warm and professional / upbeat and modern].

After the rewrite, add a section called "Facts changed or added" listing any place where your wording could be read as adding a new fact, so I can check it. If there are none, say "None."
lessons.explanation: Asking for a self-audit ("Facts changed or added") forces the model to flag its own risky wording rather than you having to catch it by close-reading every sentence. Explicitly allowing reordering and cutting filler, while banning new facts, gives Claude room to actually improve the copy instead of producing a timid near-copy of the original. Requesting multiple headline options separately from the body keeps you from having to regenerate the whole description just to test a different opening line.
lessons.example:
Original: "Nice condo in a great location. 2 bedrooms, 2 bathrooms. Kitchen has been updated. Comes with parking. HOA covers some utilities. Won't last long!"

Expected rewrite: something like "A light-filled 2-bedroom, 2-bathroom condo with an updated kitchen and a private balcony, steps from the building elevator, with one assigned parking spot included. HOA covers water, trash, and exterior maintenance." The "Facts changed or added" list should flag anything specific added beyond what the original stated (in this case, the model shouldn't add the balcony or elevator unless they were in the original — this is where you'd catch it).
lessons.exercise: In your own Claude account, pick one of your current listings with description copy that's over a month old and run it through this prompt.
lessons.expectedResult: A tighter, more specific rewrite plus a short, accurate list of anything you need to double-check before replacing the live listing description.
commonMistakes: Skipping the fact-diff step and publishing the rewrite straight away.
Not giving a target word count, so the rewrite comes back a different length than what your MLS field allows.
Accepting a headline option without checking your MLS character limit.
Rewriting copy that was already accurate and specific — this workflow is for generic or dated copy, not copy that's already strong.
lessons.proTip: Run this prompt on your 3 oldest active listings each week — a rewrite alone often revives buyer interest without any price change.

lessons.title: Write buyer follow-up emails after a viewing with Claude
lessons.summary: Turn quick notes from a showing into a personalized, non-pushy follow-up email that keeps the buyer engaged.
lessons.goal: Draft a personalized follow-up email to a buyer within minutes of a showing, referencing what they actually said and saw.
lessons.whyItMatters: Buyers form their impression of you in the 24 hours after a showing. Generic "just checking in!" emails get ignored; emails that reference specific reactions from the walkthrough get replies. Agents doing several showings a day rarely have time to write each one from scratch by hand, so a fast, personalized draft matters more than a perfect one.
steps: Right after (or between) showings, jot 2-3 lines of notes: buyer name, property, what they liked or disliked, any questions they asked.
Open Claude and use the follow-up prompt with your notes.
Specify the goal of the email — book a second showing, share comparable listings, or find out their timeline.
Review for tone — warm, not salesy.
Personalize the subject line if Claude's suggestion feels generic.
Send from your own email client.
lessons.prompt:
Write a follow-up email to a buyer after a home showing.

Buyer: [BUYER NAME]
Property shown: [ADDRESS / SHORT DESCRIPTION]
What they liked: [NOTES]
What concerned them or questions they asked: [NOTES]
My goal for this email: [e.g., invite them to a second showing this weekend / send similar listings / find out their decision timeline]

Rules:
- Reference at least one specific detail from what they liked or asked about — do not write generically.
- Keep it under 150 words.
- Tone: warm, helpful, no pressure tactics or urgency language ("won't last long," "act now").
- End with one clear, low-friction next step (a single question or suggested action), not multiple asks.
- Write a subject line under 8 words.

Do not invent details about the property or the buyer that I haven't given you.
lessons.explanation: Requiring a specific reference from the buyer's own reaction is what makes the email feel personal instead of templated — it's the single biggest lever for reply rates. Banning urgency language and multiple asks keeps the email from reading as pushy, which is the fastest way to lose a hesitant buyer's trust. Capping the word count matches how people actually read email on a phone between other tasks.
lessons.example:
Notes: "Marcus and Priya Chen, showed 27 Aspen Grove Lane #4B. Loved the balcony and afternoon light in the living room. Asked whether the HOA fee includes water. A little concerned there's no dedicated storage unit." Goal: invite them to a second showing this weekend.

Expected output: a short email opening with something like "It was great showing you and Priya through 4B — that afternoon light on the balcony really is one of the best features of the unit," answering (or promising to confirm) the HOA/water question, acknowledging the storage concern honestly, and closing with a single question inviting a second visit this weekend.
lessons.exercise: In your own Claude account, use notes from your most recent showing to draft a follow-up email with this prompt, then send it (after your own review) to that buyer.
lessons.expectedResult: A specific, warm follow-up email under 150 words with one clear next step, sent within the same day as the showing.
commonMistakes: Writing generic templates without any buyer-specific detail, which reads as mass email.
Including multiple calls to action, which makes it harder for the buyer to respond to any of them.
Using urgency or scarcity language that feels pushy on a first follow-up.
Sending without verifying any factual claim (like an HOA detail) that you weren't fully sure of.
lessons.proTip: Keep a running "showing notes" note on your phone so you always have 2-3 lines ready to paste in before you've even left the parking lot.

lessons.title: Write seller update messages that build trust with Claude
lessons.summary: Turn a week of showing activity and feedback into a clear, honest seller update that keeps clients confident even when there's no offer yet.
lessons.goal: Produce a weekly (or post-showing) seller update message that summarizes activity and feedback honestly, including when the news is lukewarm.
lessons.whyItMatters: Sellers get anxious fast when a listing sits, and silence from their agent makes it worse. A clear, honest, well-organized update — even one reporting no offers — is one of the highest-trust-building habits in the business. Writing it by hand every week for every active listing is where consistency slips, and a structured prompt keeps the habit going without softening bad news into something misleading.
steps: Gather the week's raw data: number of showings, portal views, any feedback comments, any offers or serious interest.
Paste it into Claude using the update prompt.
Tell Claude the tone you want — reassuring but honest, not falsely optimistic.
Ask for both a short text-message version and a longer email version.
Review to make sure no negative feedback has been softened into something misleading.
Send directly to your seller.
lessons.prompt:
Write a seller update message summarizing this week's activity on their listing.

Property: [ADDRESS]
Showings this week: [NUMBER]
Online views (Zillow/MLS/portal): [NUMBER OR "not tracked"]
Buyer feedback received: [PASTE RAW FEEDBACK NOTES, e.g. "liked the kitchen, thought price was high, one buyer said yard was small"]
Offers or serious interest: [NONE / DETAILS]
Any price or strategy conversation I want to open: [OPTIONAL]

Rules:
- Report the facts above honestly, including negative feedback — do not soften, omit it, or claim more interest than what's listed.
- Do not speculate about buyer intentions beyond what the feedback states.
- Tone: calm, professional, reassuring without being falsely upbeat.
- Produce two versions: (1) a text message under 400 characters, and (2) a short email (120-180 words) with a clear subject line.
- If there's a pattern in the feedback (e.g., multiple people mentioned the same thing), point it out plainly.
lessons.explanation: Explicitly forbidding softened or omitted negative feedback is the core guardrail here — sellers lose trust fast when they later learn feedback was worse than what they were told. Asking Claude to surface repeated feedback patterns turns a routine update into an early warning system for a pricing or staging conversation you need to have anyway. Producing both a text and an email version matches how sellers actually want to hear from you — quick updates by text, more detail by email.
lessons.example:
Seller: the Ortega family. Property: 27 Aspen Grove Lane #4B. Showings this week: 3. Feedback: two buyers liked the open layout; one buyer said the price felt high given there's no dedicated parking spot (only assigned street parking). No offers.

Expected output: an honest update that reports 3 showings and positive layout feedback, states plainly that pricing came up relative to parking without softening it, and suggests (if the agent included this field) opening a conversation about price or highlighting the parking situation differently — not a falsely upbeat "lots of interest!" message.
lessons.exercise: In your own Claude account, use this week's real showing and feedback numbers for one of your active listings to draft both versions and send the one that fits how you usually communicate with that seller.
lessons.expectedResult: A factually accurate update, in both text and email length, that a seller can trust even when the week's news wasn't exciting — with any repeated negative feedback called out clearly.
commonMistakes: Burying negative feedback at the end or softening its wording so it reads as neutral.
Letting the update imply more buyer interest than the actual numbers support.
Sending only one format when the seller would benefit from both a quick text and a detailed email.
Reusing last week's update with only the numbers changed, missing new feedback patterns.
lessons.proTip: When feedback repeats across multiple showings, that's your cue to raise a price or staging conversation — ask Claude to draft that conversation starter as a separate message, don't bury it inside the routine update.

lessons.title: Summarize property documents safely with Claude
lessons.summary: Get a plain-language summary of a disclosure, inspection report, or HOA document that flags what needs attention, without treating the summary as legal or professional advice.
lessons.goal: Get a plain-language summary of a disclosure, inspection report, or HOA document that flags what needs attention, without treating the AI's summary as a substitute for the full document or professional advice.
lessons.whyItMatters: Buyers and sellers hand agents dense PDFs — inspection reports, seller disclosures, HOA covenants — and expect a quick plain-English rundown. A good summary saves everyone time, but disclosure and inspection documents carry legal and safety weight, so the summary must stick strictly to what's in the document and clearly flag that it isn't a substitute for a licensed inspector, attorney, or the client's own reading of the full document.
lessons.beforeYouStart: Have the PDF or text of the document ready to upload or paste. Claude.ai on a paid plan supports file uploads up to 30MB per file, up to 20 files per chat.
steps: Open Claude and upload the document (or paste the text if it's short).
Use the summary prompt, which restricts Claude to the document's contents and requires a disclaimer.
Ask specifically for anything flagged as a safety issue, cost item, or repair needed.
Cross-check 2-3 of the summarized points against the original document yourself.
Share the summary with your client alongside the full original document, never instead of it.
Note in your file that the summary is a convenience tool, not the disclosure itself.
lessons.prompt:
I'm uploading/pasting a [inspection report / seller disclosure / HOA document] for a property. Summarize it for my client using only what's in the document.

Rules:
- Use only information contained in the document. Do not add general knowledge about what "usually" causes issues like this, and do not predict repair costs unless a cost is stated in the document.
- Organize the summary into: (1) Major issues / safety items, (2) Moderate issues / maintenance items, (3) Minor / cosmetic notes, (4) Anything unclear or that needs a professional to clarify.
- Quote or closely paraphrase the document's own language for anything in category 1.
- End with this exact disclaimer: "This is a plain-language summary for convenience only. It is not a substitute for reading the full document or for advice from a licensed inspector, attorney, or other qualified professional."

Document:
[PASTE OR UPLOAD DOCUMENT]
lessons.explanation: Banning repair-cost predictions and "usually" reasoning is critical here — a model asked to summarize an inspection report will otherwise happily add plausible-sounding context that isn't actually in the document, which is exactly the kind of error that creates liability. The four-category structure (major/moderate/minor/unclear) mirrors how buyers and sellers actually need to triage a report, and the required disclaimer keeps every summary you forward clearly labeled as a convenience tool rather than the document of record.
lessons.example:
Inspection report excerpt for the Aspen Grove condo notes a small water stain in the hall closet ceiling consistent with a past roof leak (repaired, no active leak found), a water heater original to the building (installed year noted in the report), and two bathroom outlets without GFCI protection.

Expected output: category 1 (Major/safety) would list the missing GFCI protection using the report's own language; category 2 (Moderate) would list the aging water heater and the past leak stain, noting the report found no active leak; category 4 would flag anything the report itself says needs further evaluation. No repair cost estimates should appear anywhere unless the report itself states one.
lessons.exercise: In your own Claude account, upload a real (or practice) inspection report or disclosure document and run this summary prompt, then check three of the summarized points against the source document yourself.
lessons.expectedResult: A categorized, plain-language summary with the required disclaimer, where every listed item can be traced back to specific language in the source document.
commonMistakes: Pasting only part of a multi-page document, producing an incomplete summary that looks complete.
Treating the summary as a substitute for the client reading the full report themselves.
Letting Claude estimate repair costs when the report itself didn't include any.
Forwarding the summary without the disclaimer or without attaching the original document.
lessons.proTip: For long HOA covenant documents, ask a targeted follow-up like "does this document mention rental restrictions or short-term rental rules?" instead of re-reading the whole thing yourself.

lessons.title: Create a property FAQ from listing details with Claude
lessons.summary: Generate a buyer-facing FAQ document for a listing that answers the questions buyers actually ask, using only verified listing facts.
lessons.goal: Generate a buyer-facing FAQ document for a listing that answers the questions buyers actually ask, using only verified listing facts.
lessons.whyItMatters: The same 10-12 questions come up at every open house and in every buyer inquiry — parking, utilities, HOA, showing instructions, pet policy. A ready FAQ sheet buyers can take home, or that you post alongside the listing, cuts down repetitive calls and helps serious buyers self-qualify faster.
steps: Gather your listing facts sheet (specs, HOA info, utilities, showing instructions) plus any known buyer questions from past showings.
Use the FAQ prompt with your facts.
Ask for 10-12 Q&As grouped by category.
Mark any question you can't answer yet as "Ask your agent" instead of letting Claude guess.
Format the result for print or a PDF handout.
Update the FAQ whenever a new recurring question comes up at a showing.
lessons.prompt:
Create a buyer FAQ sheet for this listing using only the facts below. Do not answer any question with information not provided — instead write "Ask your agent for current details" for that answer.

Listing facts:
[PASTE FACTS: address, price, beds/baths, sqft, year built, HOA fee and what it covers, parking, utilities included, showing instructions, any known restrictions]

Common buyer questions from past showings (optional):
[PASTE ANY RECURRING QUESTIONS]

Write 10-12 question-and-answer pairs grouped under three headers: "About the Property," "Costs & Fees," and "Logistics & Next Steps." Keep each answer to 1-3 sentences. Plain, friendly tone.
lessons.explanation: The explicit fallback instruction — "Ask your agent for current details" — is what prevents Claude from confidently guessing at a tax figure or HOA rule it wasn't given, which is the single biggest risk in a document buyers will read without you present. Grouping into three consistent categories makes the sheet scannable at an open house, and capping each answer at 1-3 sentences keeps it printable on a single page.
lessons.example:
Facts: 27 Aspen Grove Lane #4B, $415,000, 2 bed/2 bath, HOA $310/month covers water, trash, and exterior maintenance, one assigned parking spot, pet policy allows 2 pets under 40 lbs each, showings by appointment only.

Expected output includes Q&As like "What does the HOA fee cover?" → "$310/month, covering water, trash, and exterior building maintenance," and "Can I have a pet?" → "Yes, up to 2 pets under 40 lbs each are allowed." A question like "What are the property taxes?" should return "Ask your agent for current details" since no tax figure was in the facts.
lessons.exercise: In your own Claude account, build a facts list for one of your current listings and generate the FAQ sheet with this prompt, then print or save it as a PDF handout.
lessons.expectedResult: A one-page, print-ready FAQ sheet grouped into three clear categories, with any unanswerable question honestly flagged rather than guessed at.
commonMistakes: Letting the AI guess at HOA fees, taxes, or square footage instead of flagging them as unknown.
Making the FAQ too long — buyers won't read past a single page at an open house.
Not updating the sheet after a new recurring question shows up at a showing.
Forgetting to verify the numbers are still current before reprinting for a new open house.
lessons.proTip: Keep one master facts-sheet template and just swap in new listing details each time — it turns this into a 3-minute task per listing instead of a fresh write-up.

lessons.title: Write neighborhood guide copy grounded in verified facts with Claude
lessons.summary: Produce neighborhood guide copy for a listing or website that only uses facts you've verified, clearly separating verified content from anything that needs a source check.
lessons.goal: Produce neighborhood guide copy for a listing or website that only uses facts you've verified, clearly separating verified content from anything that needs a source check.
lessons.whyItMatters: Neighborhood copy — "top-rated schools," "5 minutes to downtown," "walkable to shops" — is one of the highest-risk categories of real estate content, because it's exactly the kind of specific, checkable claim an AI will confidently invent if you let it. School ratings, commute times, and safety claims change and vary by exact address; getting one wrong is a credibility hit with a buyer who checks it themselves, and can be a genuine fair-housing risk if the copy strays into describing who lives somewhere rather than what's there. This lesson teaches you to draft engaging copy from facts you supply, and to have Claude flag gaps rather than fill them in silently.
lessons.beforeYouStart: Verify your own core facts first — walk score, actual measured drive times, nearby named amenities. This lesson is about drafting persuasive copy from verified facts, not researching them from scratch (see the Gemini Deep Research market-research lesson for sourcing help).
steps: Assemble your verified facts list: named nearby amenities, actual drive/walk times you've measured, park and transit info, general neighborhood character notes.
Use the guide prompt, explicitly banning invented statistics, school ratings, and safety claims.
Ask for two lengths: a short listing blurb (60-80 words) and a longer standalone guide (250-300 words).
Review word-for-word for any specific number, ranking, or claim you didn't supply.
Never let Claude write about school quality, safety, or demographics unless you supply a specific, sourced fact and can point to its source.
Publish only the version you've fact-checked.
lessons.prompt:
Write neighborhood guide copy for a listing, using only the facts I provide below.

Strict rules:
- Use only the facts listed. Do not add school ratings, crime/safety claims, demographic statements, walk scores, or specific distances/times that I haven't given you.
- If you think a detail would strengthen the copy but I haven't provided it, list it separately under "Facts I'd need to add this" — don't write it into the copy.
- Avoid any language that could be read as describing a neighborhood in terms of who lives there; describe places and amenities, not people or "types" of residents.
- Tone: warm, specific, sensory where the facts allow it, no generic filler like "vibrant community."

Neighborhood: [NEIGHBORHOOD NAME]
Verified facts:
[PASTE: named nearby amenities, measured drive/walk times, transit access, parks, notable nearby businesses, general character notes]

Write:
1. A 60-80 word version for the listing description.
2. A 250-300 word standalone neighborhood guide for the website.
lessons.explanation: Naming the exact forbidden categories — school ratings, crime claims, demographic statements, walk scores — is more effective than a general "stick to the facts" instruction, because those are precisely the categories models tend to fill in from general knowledge when a neighborhood name is recognizable. The fair-housing instruction is placed as a standing rule, not a one-time reminder, since it applies to every sentence, not just an obvious one. Requesting a "Facts I'd need to add this" list turns the model's urge to embellish into a useful research to-do list instead of a risk.
lessons.example:
Willow Creek neighborhood facts: 6-minute walk to Willow Creek Park, which hosts a weekend farmers market April through October; 12-minute drive to downtown (measured at midday); a grocery store and two coffee shops within a half-mile; a dedicated bike lane running along Aspen Grove Lane.

Expected output: a short blurb mentioning the park, farmers market, and walkability to coffee/grocery, and a longer guide that expands on those same verified points sensorially (e.g., describing the Saturday market rather than adding an invented walk score). Any school, safety, or demographic claim should be entirely absent unless supplied.
lessons.exercise: In your own Claude account, gather verified facts for one neighborhood you sell in and generate both the short and long versions, checking each sentence against your facts list before using either.
lessons.expectedResult: Two lengths of neighborhood copy, entirely traceable to facts you personally verified, with no invented statistics, ratings, or claims about who lives in the area.
commonMistakes: Letting a "great schools nearby" or similar claim slip through unverified.
Using drive or walk times you haven't personally measured or sourced.
Language that inadvertently steers based on the type of resident an area might suit — a fair-housing risk.
Publishing the guide before fact-checking every specific number against its source.
lessons.proTip: Build a standing "verified neighborhood facts" document per area you sell in — most facts like parks, transit, and walk times don't change often, so you fact-check once and reuse the file for every new listing in that area.

lessons.title: Write multi-platform social posts for a new listing with Claude
lessons.summary: Turn one new listing into a set of platform-appropriate social posts — Instagram, Facebook, LinkedIn, and a short-video script — from a single source brief.
lessons.goal: Turn one new listing into a set of platform-appropriate social posts (Instagram, Facebook, LinkedIn, and a short-video script) from a single source brief.
lessons.whyItMatters: New listings need to go out everywhere within hours of hitting the market, but a caption that works on Instagram reads wrong on LinkedIn, and a good static post isn't a video script. Writing four or five versions by hand for every listing is where social marketing quietly stops happening. A single grounded brief that fans out into platform-native drafts keeps a consistent posting habit without repetitive work.
steps: Write one short source brief: address, key features, price (if public), any open house details.
Use the multi-platform prompt with that brief.
Ask for platform-specific formatting to be respected — hashtag conventions, caption length, tone shift for LinkedIn versus Instagram.
Review each draft against your MLS/brokerage rules on what can be publicly stated (price, address format, fair housing language).
Add your own photos or video before posting — the prompt doesn't generate images.
Schedule posts across a few days rather than dumping them all at once.
lessons.prompt:
Create social media posts announcing a new listing, using only the facts below. Do not invent features, price, or availability details not listed.

Listing facts:
[PASTE: address or neighborhood, beds/baths, standout features, price if public, open house date/time if any, your contact info]

Write:
1. Instagram caption (under 150 words, casual-warm tone, 5-8 relevant hashtags, one clear call to action)
2. Facebook post (slightly longer, more conversational, suited to a local community audience, include open house details if provided)
3. LinkedIn post (professional tone, framed around market context or the value of the listing rather than hype, no hashtag spam — 2-3 max)
4. A 30-second short-video voiceover script (for a walkthrough reel), written in short spoken sentences with [VISUAL: ...] cues for what to show at each line

Include required fair-housing-safe language throughout: describe the property and location, never the type of buyer or resident it would suit.
lessons.explanation: Generating all four formats from one brief in a single pass keeps the underlying facts identical across platforms, so you're not re-explaining the listing each time and risking drift between versions. Naming the tone shift per platform explicitly (casual on Instagram, professional and context-driven on LinkedIn) gets you posts that don't read like the same caption pasted three times. The fair-housing instruction is repeated here for the same reason as in the neighborhood-guide lesson — social copy is public-facing and easy to publish without a second review.
lessons.example:
Brief: new listing 27 Aspen Grove Lane #4B, 2BR/2BA condo, $415,000, open house Saturday 1-3pm, standout features are a private balcony, in-unit washer/dryer, and reserved parking.

Expected output: an Instagram caption leading with the balcony and open house time with a "link in bio" CTA; a Facebook post inviting the local community to the open house with more conversational detail; a LinkedIn post framing the listing around current local market context; and a video script opening on the balcony with a [VISUAL: balcony, afternoon light] cue, moving through the kitchen and laundry, closing on a call to action.
lessons.exercise: In your own Claude account, write a brief for a current or recent listing and generate all four post formats, then review each against your brokerage's compliance rules before posting.
lessons.expectedResult: Four platform-ready drafts from one brief, each following its platform's conventions, with your own photos or video added before anything is published.
commonMistakes: Posting AI-suggested hashtags or claims without checking brokerage compliance rules first.
Copy-pasting the same caption to every platform instead of using the platform-specific versions.
Using steering language (e.g., "perfect for young professionals") that creates fair-housing risk.
Forgetting to include a call to action or contact info in the final published post.
lessons.proTip: Keep your brief format identical every time — same fields, same order — so this becomes a 5-minute paste-and-review task instead of a 20-minute writing task for every new listing.

lessons.title: Build objection-handling scripts and negotiation talking points with Claude
lessons.summary: Generate practice scripts for common buyer or seller objections and negotiation moments, tailored to a specific deal situation.
lessons.goal: Generate practice scripts for common buyer/seller objections and negotiation moments, tailored to the real facts of a specific deal.
lessons.whyItMatters: The moments that make or break a deal — "the price is too high," "I want to wait for rates to drop," "the other agent's offer terms are better" — happen live, on the phone or in person, with no time to think. Rehearsing responses ahead of time, grounded in the actual facts of your deal rather than generic scripts, is how experienced agents stay calm and credible under pressure.
steps: Describe the specific objection or negotiation moment you're preparing for, plus the real facts of the situation.
Use the script prompt to generate 2-3 response approaches, not just one.
Ask for the reasoning behind each approach so you know when to use which.
Practice out loud — ask Claude to roleplay the other side pushing back further.
Adjust the scripts to your own voice; don't memorize them word for word.
Save the approaches that worked well as your personal playbook.
lessons.prompt:
Help me prepare for a negotiation conversation in a real estate deal.

Situation: [DESCRIBE: e.g., buyer says the list price is too high; seller is refusing to negotiate on inspection repairs; competing offer has a shorter closing timeline]
My role: [buyer's agent / seller's agent]
Relevant facts I can reference: [PASTE: comps, inspection findings, market conditions, client's actual constraints/priorities — only real ones]
What I want to achieve: [GOAL]

Give me:
1. Two or three different response approaches (e.g., data-led, empathy-led, options-led), each 3-5 sentences of talking points, not a rigid script to read verbatim.
2. A one-line explanation of when each approach fits best.
3. One likely pushback for each approach and how I could respond.

Do not invent comps, numbers, or facts about the deal beyond what I've given you — if I haven't given you a number, use a placeholder like [YOUR COMP DATA] instead of a made-up figure.

Then roleplay the other party pushing back on my strongest approach so I can practice responding.
lessons.explanation: Asking for talking points rather than a verbatim script keeps the output usable in the moment — a memorized script falls apart the instant the conversation goes off-path, but internalized approaches adapt. Requiring multiple approaches with guidance on when to use each builds actual judgment rather than a single canned answer. The roleplay step is what turns this from a reading exercise into practice, and explicitly banning invented comps or numbers keeps you from accidentally citing a figure in a live negotiation that you can't back up.
lessons.example:
Situation: a buyer says $415,000 for the Aspen Grove condo feels high compared to a similar 2BR unit two floors down that sold for $395,000 last month. Role: seller's agent. Facts: the lower unit had no balcony and an original kitchen; this unit has a renovated kitchen and a private balcony.

Expected output: a data-led approach citing the specific differences (balcony, renovated kitchen) as the price gap's explanation; an empathy-led approach acknowledging the buyer's price sensitivity while reframing value; an options-led approach exploring other terms (closing date, minor concessions) instead of price alone — each with a likely pushback and response.
lessons.exercise: In your own Claude account, prepare for a real upcoming negotiation conversation using your own deal facts, then have Claude roleplay the toughest pushback so you can practice out loud.
lessons.expectedResult: Two or three practiced, deal-specific response approaches you can adapt in your own words, plus at least one round of practiced pushback-and-response before the real conversation happens.
commonMistakes: Letting Claude supply comp numbers or figures instead of using your own verified data.
Memorizing a script verbatim instead of internalizing the approach, which sounds robotic in the room.
Skipping the roleplay/practice step and only reading the talking points silently.
Choosing an approach that doesn't match your natural communication style just because it reads well on the page.
lessons.proTip: Ask Claude to roleplay the toughest version of the other side's pushback, not the easy version — that's the practice that actually helps when the real conversation gets difficult.

lessons.title: Local market research with Gemini Deep Research
lessons.summary: Get a cited, verifiable snapshot of current local market conditions — inventory, price trends, days on market — to support a listing presentation or buyer conversation.
lessons.goal: Get a cited, verifiable snapshot of current local market conditions (inventory, price trends, days on market) to support a listing presentation or buyer conversation.
lessons.whyItMatters: Clients increasingly fact-check what their agent tells them, and market-condition claims — "inventory is tight right now," "prices are up this quarter" — are exactly the kind of thing worth citing rather than asserting. Gemini Deep Research browses many sources and returns a cited report, so you can hand a client both the summary and the underlying links, a level of credibility a plain chat answer doesn't give you.
lessons.beforeYouStart: Have a Gemini account (gemini.google.com). Deep Research is free on the Flash tier; Google AI Pro (about $19.99/mo) raises the quota and uses the stronger Gemini 3.1 Pro model, worth it if you run this often.
steps: Open the Gemini app and start a Deep Research session rather than a normal chat, so it runs genuine multi-step web research instead of a single quick answer.
Ask a specific, scoped market question — name the exact area and timeframe, not just "the market."
Review the research plan Gemini proposes before it runs, and adjust it if it's missing a data point you need.
Wait for the report — Deep Research browses many sources over several minutes, it isn't instant like a regular chat reply.
Read the cited sources in the report, not just the summary — click through 2-3 to confirm they're recent and locally specific.
Ask a follow-up narrowing to your exact segment (e.g., condos vs. single-family, a specific price band).
Export or copy the findings into a short client-ready summary with the source links kept visible.
Note the date you ran the research — market data ages fast, so re-run it before reusing it in a new conversation.
lessons.prompt:
Research current housing market conditions for [NEIGHBORHOOD/CITY/ZIP], focusing on the last [TIMEFRAME, e.g. "quarter" or "3 months"].

I need, with sources for each:
1. Median sale price and how it has changed over the timeframe
2. Average days on market
3. Current inventory levels (active listings) and how that compares to the prior period
4. Whether it currently favors buyers or sellers, and why
5. Any notable recent trend specific to this area (new construction, rate changes affecting local demand, etc.)

Focus on [PROPERTY TYPE, e.g., condos / single-family homes] specifically if the data allows it. Cite each figure with its source and the date the source was published. Flag if you can't find area-specific data and had to widen the search to a larger region.
lessons.explanation: Naming a specific area and timeframe rather than asking about "the market" is what gets Gemini Deep Research to run genuinely local queries instead of returning national headline numbers. Deep Research browses many sources over several minutes and returns a cited report — reviewing the plan it proposes before it runs, and requiring a source and publish date on every figure, is what gives you the citation trail to hand a client directly. The instruction to flag when it had to widen the search keeps you from unknowingly presenting regional data as neighborhood-specific.
lessons.example: Query scoped to "Willow Creek neighborhood, condo market, last quarter" should return a cited summary with median price and its change, average days on market, current active inventory versus the prior quarter, a buyer's- or seller's-market read with reasoning, and a note if it had to fall back to city-wide data for any figure — each line backed by a linked, dated source.
lessons.exercise: In your own Gemini account, run this research for a neighborhood or ZIP code you currently work in, and click through at least two citations yourself to verify they're recent and locally specific.
lessons.expectedResult: A cited market snapshot you could hand directly to a client, with every figure traceable to a dated source, and a clear note of the date you ran the research.
commonMistakes: Trusting the summary paragraph without opening any of the citations.
Asking a question too broad to get locally specific data, such as "how's the market" with no area or timeframe.
Treating Deep Research like an instant chat reply and closing the tab before the report finishes running.
Reusing month-old research in a new client conversation as if it's current.
lessons.proTip: Create a Gem with your standard market-research prompt and format saved as standing instructions, one per market area you cover — it turns a one-off search into a habit you can repeat every week in a couple of minutes, and Deep Research reports can be exported straight to Google Docs for a client-ready file.

lessons.title: Organize lead notes and build a weekly sales activity report with Claude
lessons.summary: Turn a week's worth of scattered lead notes and activity numbers into an organized lead list and a clean weekly activity report.
lessons.goal: Turn a week's worth of scattered lead notes and activity into an organized lead list and a clean weekly activity report for yourself or your broker.
lessons.whyItMatters: Leads pile up across texts, calls, open-house sign-ins, and portal inquiries, and without a regular pass to organize them, warm leads go cold. Brokers and team leads also often require a weekly activity report — a task that eats time agents would rather spend prospecting. Turning raw, messy notes into a structured list and report is a repetitive but necessary task well suited to a constrained prompt.
steps: Collect the week's raw lead notes and activity numbers (calls made, showings held, new leads, offers written) in one place, even if messy.
Use the organizing prompt to turn raw lead notes into a structured table.
Review the priority or next-action Claude suggested for each lead and adjust based on your own judgment.
Use the second part of the prompt to generate the weekly activity report from the same raw numbers.
Cross-check the totals in the report against your source notes before sending.
Send the report to your broker or team lead, and use the lead table to plan next week's follow-ups.
lessons.prompt:
I have messy notes on leads from this week. Organize them into a table using only the information I provide — do not guess at a lead's likely budget, timeline, or interest level unless I've stated it.

Raw lead notes:
[PASTE: names, how they contacted you, what they said, any info on budget/timeline/property interest]

Create a table with columns: Name, Source (call/text/open house/portal), What they're looking for, Stated timeline (or "not stated"), Last contact, Suggested next action.
For "Suggested next action," base it only on what's stated — e.g., if no timeline was given, suggest a next action that would find out the timeline rather than assuming urgency.

Then, using these activity numbers: [PASTE: calls made, showings held, new leads, offers written, closings], write a 100-150 word weekly activity summary in a professional tone suitable for a broker or team lead, reporting the numbers as given without embellishment.
lessons.explanation: The instruction to suggest a fact-finding next action (rather than an urgency-based one) whenever a timeline is missing is the key guardrail — it stops the model from inventing false urgency for a lead who never expressed any, which would send you chasing the wrong people. Keeping the table format identical every week (same six columns) makes it easy to scan and to compare against last week's list. Asking for the activity report from the same raw numbers, with no embellishment, keeps the report a factual record your broker can trust rather than a sales pitch.
lessons.example:
Lead notes: "Jordan T. — called Tuesday, said looking for 3BR under $450k, no timeline given" and "the Alvarez family — open-house sign-in Saturday, said moving from out of state by end of year." Activity numbers: 22 calls, 6 showings, 3 new leads, 1 offer written.

Expected output: a table row for Jordan T. with "Stated timeline: not stated" and a next action like "call to ask about timeline and financing status," not an assumption of urgency; a row for the Alvarez family noting the end-of-year timeline and a next action suited to that pace. The activity summary should report the 22/6/3/1 figures plainly in a short paragraph.
lessons.exercise: In your own Claude account, gather this week's real lead notes and activity numbers and generate both the lead table and the weekly report using this prompt.
lessons.expectedResult: A clean, scannable lead table with honest next actions, and a factual weekly activity summary ready to send to a broker or team lead, with every number checked against your source notes.
commonMistakes: Letting the AI assign urgency or priority to a lead who never stated a timeline.
Padding the activity report with numbers that weren't actually in your notes.
Inconsistent note-taking during the week, which makes the organizing pass much less useful.
Generating the report and table but never actually acting on the suggested next-action column.
lessons.proTip: Keep a single running document for the week's raw lead notes as you go — even one line per contact — so this becomes a 5-minute Friday task instead of a reconstruction project.

lessons.title: Build a simple property landing page with Codex
lessons.summary: Use Codex to generate a working single-page property landing site — hero, gallery placeholders, details, contact form — that you can customize and host for a listing.
lessons.goal: Use Codex to generate a working single-page property landing site (hero, gallery placeholders, details, contact form) that you can customize and host for a listing.
lessons.whyItMatters: A dedicated landing page for a listing — with its own shareable link, ideal for ad campaigns, QR codes on yard signs, and open-house sign-ins — outperforms a generic portal listing for capturing lead contact info. Building one from scratch with a web developer is overkill for a single listing; a coding agent can produce a clean, working page from a plain-language brief in one sitting, provided you review what it generates before publishing anything live.
lessons.beforeYouStart: Install Codex CLI (`npm i -g @openai/codex` or the platform installer) and sign in with your ChatGPT account, or use the Codex Cloud/web interface at chatgpt.com/codex. Basic comfort running terminal commands helps but isn't required if you use the web version. Have your listing facts and photos ready to drop in.
steps: Start a new Codex session in an empty project folder (`codex` in the terminal, or a new task in Codex Cloud connected to a repo).
Give Codex the landing-page brief below, filled in with your real listing facts.
Let Codex generate the page, then review the diff and files before accepting — read the HTML/CSS/JS it produced, don't just trust the preview.
Ask Codex to swap in your real photos and contact form details once you've reviewed the structure.
Test the page locally (open the HTML file, or run the suggested local server command) and check it at a narrow browser width to confirm it's mobile-responsive.
Ask Codex to fix any specific issue you spot (e.g., "the contact form doesn't validate email format") rather than regenerating the whole page.
Deploy using a static host of your choice — the platform doesn't provide hosting — and put the link on your yard sign QR code and ads.
lessons.prompt:
Build a simple, single-page property landing site as static HTML/CSS/JS (no framework needed). Use only the facts below — do not invent property details, and use clearly labeled placeholder text like [PHOTO 1] for images I'll add myself.

Property facts:
[PASTE: address, price, beds/baths, sqft, 3-5 standout features, open house date if any]
Agent contact info: [NAME, PHONE, EMAIL, BROKERAGE]

Requirements:
1. Hero section with property headline, price, and a primary photo placeholder
2. Photo gallery section with 6-8 placeholder image slots
3. Details section listing the specs and standout features as a clean list
4. A contact form (name, email, phone, message) that validates required fields client-side and is ready for me to wire up to my own email/CRM endpoint — add a clear code comment showing where to plug that in
5. Mobile-responsive layout (test at 375px and 1440px widths)
6. Fast-loading: no heavy dependencies, semantic HTML, basic on-page SEO (title tag, meta description) using only the facts provided

After building it, tell me which files you created and how to preview it locally.
lessons.explanation: Specifying "static HTML/CSS/JS, no framework needed" keeps the output something you can actually review and host cheaply without needing a build pipeline you'd have to maintain. Requiring a labeled comment at the contact-form integration point, instead of a fake working backend, is what keeps the page honest about what it does and doesn't do until you wire it up yourself. Asking Codex to name the files it created and how to preview them turns the session into something you can verify rather than a black box you have to trust.
lessons.example: Brief for the Aspen Grove condo: 27 Aspen Grove Lane, Unit 4B, $415,000, 2BR/2BA, private balcony, in-unit washer/dryer, reserved parking, open house Saturday 1-3pm. Expected result: Codex scaffolds files such as index.html, styles.css, and script.js, with the hero section reading "27 Aspen Grove Lane, Unit 4B — $415,000," a gallery of labeled photo placeholders, a details list of the stated features, and a contact form with client-side validation and a clearly commented spot to add a real form endpoint.
lessons.exercise: In your own Codex account or project, run this brief for one of your active listings using its real facts and your own contact details, then preview the generated page locally and check it at both a phone-width and desktop-width viewport before making any further changes.
lessons.expectedResult: A working local static site with the six required sections, previewable in a browser, reviewed file-by-file by you before any deployment or use with real client contact information.
commonMistakes: Accepting generated code without reading it, especially how the contact form handles submitted data.
Deploying with placeholder or sample contact info accidentally left in the page.
Skipping the mobile-width check and only reviewing the page at desktop size.
Asking Codex to regenerate the entire page for a small fix instead of requesting a targeted change.
lessons.proTip: Keep the property facts and agent-info block in a small reusable text file — building a new listing's landing page becomes a matter of swapping that file and rerunning the same brief.
